Stroke mortality: scraping tables and citations from a PMC HTML article

Source: vignettes/html-scraping.Rmd
html-scraping.Rmd
library(bst260projhelp)

The other two vignettes work from PDF reports. This one works from a journal article published only as HTML – a PMC page bundled with the package – and shows a third kind of information transformation: rvest-based scraping instead of pdftools-based extraction.

article <- bst260_example("PMC13794488.html")

Information transformation: scraping structure out of PMC’s HTML

PMC renders every article against the same handful of conventions: standard citation_* meta tags in the <head> (the Highwire Press/Google Scholar scheme most publishing platforms emit), and predictable element ids in the body (TabN for tables, FigN for figures, AbsN for the abstract, CRN for reference-list entries). None of the functions below are specific to this one paper – they read those conventions, not anything peculiar to this article.

Article metadata, straight from the <head> 

meta <- html_article_meta(article)
meta[c("title", "journal", "volume", "date", "doi", "pmid")]
#> $title
#> [1] "Trends and disparities in stroke mortality with diabetes as a contributing cause among U.S. adults, 1999–2023: a uniform-definition national analysis of long-term decline and a post-2014, pandemic-era increase"
#> 
#> $journal
#> [1] "BMC Public Health"
#> 
#> $volume
#> [1] "26"
#> 
#> $date
#> [1] "2026 Aug 31"
#> 
#> $doi
#> [1] "10.1186/s12889-026-29268-y"
#> 
#> $pmid
#> [1] "43073902"
meta$authors
#> [1] "Yan Cheng"    "Ji Li"        "Yunzhou Yang"

Finding and reading a table

Unlike a PDF, where a table has no machine-readable boundary and has to be found by its caption text, an HTML table is a real <table> element – but it still needs to be found correctly: PMC wraps each table together with its caption in an enclosing <section>, and calling rvest::html_table() on that wrapper (rather than drilling down to the actual <table> inside it) silently produces a nonsense one-row pseudo-table instead of erroring. html_table_index() lists what’s there; html_read_table() does the drill-down correctly:

html_table_index(article)[c("id", "label")]
#>     id    label
#> 1 Tab1 Table 1.
#> 2 Tab2 Table 2.

Table 2 reports the paper’s own segmented-regression estimates, and its column names are the paper’s abbreviations, not self-explanatory labels, so they’re worth spelling out before the table appears rather than after:

  • change point – the year, estimated from the data rather than assumed, at which the trend in mortality significantly shifts.
  • APC (annual percentage change) – the constant yearly rate of change within one segment of the trend (e.g. before vs. after the change point).
  • AAPC (average annual percentage change) – a single summary rate across the whole 1999-2023 period, averaging the early- and late-period APCs in proportion to how many years each segment spans.
tab2 <- html_read_table(article, "Tab2")
dtab(tab2)

Abstract and a cited figure 

ab <- html_abstract(article)
names(ab)
#> [1] "Background"  "Methods"     "Results"     "Conclusions"
ab[["Background"]]
#> [1] "Diabetes mellitus is a major contributor to cerebrovascular risk and stroke-related mortality. Although U.S. cardiovascular mortality declined for decades, national estimates for stroke mortality among people with diabetes have been inconsistent, partly because of differences in case definition and in the handling of the 2018 change in population race classification."

Figures are harder to extract “as text” than tables are, since the data they summarize was never in the HTML at all – but the image itself is: PMC serves it from its own CDN, so html_figure_image() just needs the <img> element’s src, not a download. article is licensed CC BY 4.0 (confirmed below, straight from the page’s own licence statement), so it can be reproduced here with attribution rather than only described:

fig1 <- html_figure_image(article, "Fig1")
knitr::include_graphics(fig1$src)

cap <- html_figure_caption(article, "Fig1")
meta <- html_article_meta(article)
cat(sprintf(
  "**Fig. 1.** %s\n\n*Source:* %s. %s. *%s*. %s;%s:%s. [%s](https://doi.org/%s). Licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).",
  cap, paste(meta$authors, collapse = ", "), meta$title, meta$journal,
  substr(meta$date, 1, 4), meta$volume, meta$firstpage, meta$doi, meta$doi
))

Fig. 1. National age-adjusted mortality rate for stroke (underlying cause; ICD-10 I60–I69) with diabetes (E10–E14) as a contributing cause, U.S. adults ≥ 25 years, 1999–2023. Points show observed rates with a 95% CI band; the red line shows the fitted segmented model, with the change point at 2014 (dotted line) and the 2014 nadir (4.28 per 100,000) marked. Segment annual percentage changes (APCs) with 95% confidence intervals are annotated (* P < 0.05). The shaded band denotes the 2020–2021 pandemic-peak years

Source: Yan Cheng, Ji Li, Yunzhou Yang. Trends and disparities in stroke mortality with diabetes as a contributing cause among U.S. adults, 1999–2023: a uniform-definition national analysis of long-term decline and a post-2014, pandemic-era increase. BMC Public Health. 2026;26:3518. 10.1186/s12889-026-29268-y. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Both the table- and figure-extraction functions above are generic in the same sense the PDF ones are: nothing about them is specific to stroke, diabetes, or this journal – the same calls work on any PMC article that follows these id and meta-tag conventions.

Bibliographic integrity: a reference list PMC has already structured

This paper cites by number – [1], [1, 2] – against a 21-entry reference list. Unlike the RAND and CDC reports, where the reference list is plain PDF text that first has to be parsed back into structure, PMC’s own HTML has already done that: each entry is a <li id="CRN"> carrying a formatted citation plus direct links to its DOI and PubMed record, and every in-text citation marker is itself a real link, <a href="#CRN">, straight to its entry – not text that merely looks like a citation. So pmc_ref_entries() and pmc_find_citations() are reads, not parsers:

refs <- pmc_ref_entries(article)
nrow(refs)
#> [1] 21
refs[1:3, c("key", "text", "doi")]
#>   key
#> 1 CR1
#> 2 CR2
#> 3 CR3
#>                                                                                                                                                                         text
#> 1    Tsao CW, Aday AW, Almarzooq ZI, et al. Heart disease and stroke statistics—2023 update: a report from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2023;147(8):e93–621.
#> 2 Virani SS, Alonso A, Aparicio HJ, et al. Heart disease and stroke statistics—2021 update: a report from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2021;143(8):e254–743.
#> 3                              Gregg EW, Li Y, Wang J, et al. Changes in diabetes-related complications in the United States, 1990–2010. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(16):1514–23.
#>                            doi
#> 1 10.1161/CIR.0000000000001123
#> 2 10.1161/CIR.0000000000000950
#> 3        10.1056/NEJMoa1310799

cites <- pmc_find_citations(article)
nrow(cites)
#> [1] 30
head(cites)
#>   para key label
#> 1 Par5 CR1     1
#> 2 Par5 CR2     2
#> 3 Par5 CR1     1
#> 4 Par5 CR3     3
#> 5 Par5 CR4     4
#> 6 Par5 CR5     5

Cross-checking the citations

Because every in-text marker is already a structural link, checking that it resolves to a real entry is just a set-membership test – no heuristic regex over plain text, the way [vancouver_find_numeric_citations()] has to work:

stopifnot(all(cites$key %in% refs$key))

Each citation link gets its own anchor id, via the same [bib_cite_link()] used for the RAND and CDC vignettes, so it can link down to its entry and that entry can link back up to every place it was cited:

cite_id <- paste0("cite-", cites$key, "-", seq_len(nrow(cites)))
cites$link <- bib_cite_link(cites$key, label = cites$label, id = cite_id)
cited_at <- split(cite_id, cites$key)
dtab(cites[c("para", "key", "link")], escape = FALSE)

The rendered bibliography

pmc_bibliography_html() is a thin wrapper around the same [bib_html_list()] renderer the RAND and CDC vignettes use – PMC’s entries arrive already formatted with their own DOI and a PubMed fallback URL, so there’s no formatting step first. Every entry links to its DOI on doi.org; the small &uarr; links back up to every place in the text it was actually cited:

cat(pmc_bibliography_html(refs, cited_at), sep = "\n")
  1. Tsao CW, Aday AW, Almarzooq ZI, et al. Heart disease and stroke statistics—2023 update: a report from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2023;147(8):e93–621. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001123 ↑ ↑

table(has_doi = !is.na(refs$doi))
#> has_doi
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>     5    16

Most entries have a DOI linked directly in PMC’s own HTML, but not all – a handful (e.g. government data-brief and surveillance-report citations) have neither a DOI nor a PubMed record, and are correctly marked no DOI above rather than silently dropped, the same guarantee [bib_html_list()] makes for the RAND and CDC vignettes.
